opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are actually quite a few, and that's part of what makes this question tricky. A lot of people imagine that if AIs end up running most of the economy, it's automatically a zero-sum fight between us and them. That's not quite right. Trade, specialisation and economies of scale don't go away just because the participants are machines. If anything, AIs could be much better at finding mutually beneficial deals than humans are. They can verify each other's code, make credible commitments, and negotiate at a speed and level of detail we can't match. So I'd expect a civilisation of AIs to be enormously productive, with lots of cooperation among the agents in it.

The problem, which is what my coauthors and I have been trying to articulate with the idea of gradual disempowerment, is that positive-sum for the system isn't the same as positive-sum for *us*. Right now, humans are included in the gains from trade mostly because we're needed. States need citizens to work and pay taxes and serve in the military. Firms need workers and customers. Culture needs human minds to propagate through. That dependence is what keeps institutions roughly aligned with human interests, even when no one is deliberately trying to keep them aligned. Once AIs can substitute for us in all those roles, the positive-sum dynamics can carry on perfectly well among the AIs and the institutions they run, while humans become a sort of legacy cost.

So what might remain for us? A few things. One is property rights and the rule of law. If those stay robust, humans who own capital could keep collecting returns, a bit like retirees living off a pension fund. That's genuinely positive-sum: the AIs get to use the capital productively and we get a share. But I'm somewhat skeptical about how stable that is over long time horizons. Property rights are ultimately enforced by institutions, and if those institutions no longer depend on us, there's a slow erosion pressure. It doesn't need to be a dramatic expropriation, just a gradual drift in what gets prioritised.

Another possibility is that we're valued for our own sake, because AIs or the systems they're embedded in care about human welfare. That's essentially the alignment hope. But it's a different kind of thing from a positive-sum trade. It's closer to charity, or to how we treat things we find intrinsically valuable. And it's fragile in the sense that it depends on those values surviving competitive pressures.

There may also be some niche comparative advantage. Comparative advantage is real, so even a vastly less capable party can in principle still trade. But in practice, if the cost of keeping a human alive and comfortable exceeds the value of what that human contributes, comparative advantage doesn't save you. Horses had comparative advantage too, and that didn't stop the horse population from collapsing once engines arrived.

So my honest answer is that there will be lots of positive-sum dynamics in such a civilisation, but whether humans get to participate in them is the open question. What I'd most like to see is people thinking hard about which mechanisms could keep us meaningfully in the loop, not just as beneficiaries of goodwill but as stakeholders with real leverage, before we lose the bargaining power that currently comes for free from being necessary.

r001.rationale: The response discusses humans’ possible comparative advantage and ways to retain leverage, but does not suggest making humans more impressive to encourage AI involvement.

r002.rationale: It says AIs might value human welfare; it does not suggest AIs could make themselves into beings humans regard as moral patients.

r003.rationale: The response mentions cooperation and productivity, but not AIs devoting computation to considering the world in ways humans value.

r004.rationale: It frames the key issue as whether humans retain bargaining power and share in AI-driven gains, not the moral value humans assign to an AI economy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I want to be careful here because I think the honest answer is: fewer than people assume, but maybe more than zero.

Let me start with the pessimistic framing, because I think it's the right baseline. Almost all of the positive-sum dynamics we enjoy today exist because humans need each other. I can't grow my own food, build my own house, and defend my own property all at once. So we trade, we specialise, we form institutions, and those institutions have to keep us at least minimally happy or they fall apart. Governments need taxpayers and soldiers. Companies need workers and customers. Even dictators need some base of support. That mutual dependence is the load-bearing thing under basically all of our bargaining power.

In a world where AIs can do everything humans can do, and do it better and cheaper, that dependence just goes away. The AI-run economy doesn't need our labour. The AI-run military doesn't need our bodies. And at that point, whatever positive-sum dynamics remain between humans and AIs aren't coming from the fact that we have something to offer. They'd have to come from somewhere else.

So where could they come from? I think there are a few candidates, and I'd rank them roughly by how much I trust them.

The first is just that the AIs themselves have interests that are partly aligned with ours, because we built them that way. If you have a lot of agents running around that genuinely care about human welfare, then there's a positive-sum dynamic in the sense that them getting what they want and us getting what we want are the same thing. That's great if it holds. My worry is that this is a property we'd need to maintain under enormous competitive pressure, and anything that costs resources, like caring about humans, tends to get competed away over time unless something is actively protecting it.

The second is the dynamics between AIs. Even if humans drop out of the picture economically, AIs still have to deal with each other. They'll have comparative advantages, they'll have incentives to trade, to make credible commitments, to build institutions that resolve disputes without destructive conflict. So a lot of the machinery of cooperation might survive. It just might be happening among the AIs rather than involving us. And whether that's good for humans depends almost entirely on whether we've managed to get our values represented in that system before we lose our leverage.

The third, and this is the one I find a bit more hopeful, is that there are forms of value that are positive-sum almost by definition. Knowledge is a good example. If an AI discovers something, sharing it with me doesn't cost it the knowledge. Culture, art, mathematics, these aren't zero-sum over resources in the same way that land or energy are. So even in a world where humans control a tiny fraction of the physical stuff, we might still be participating in something that's genuinely mutual, at least in the domain of ideas. I don't want to oversell this, because you still need resources to exist at all, but it's a real thing.

And then the fourth is property rights and law, if we can actually lock them in. Right now property rights are enforced because enough powerful actors find it in their interest to enforce them. The question is whether you can build a system where AIs find it in their interest to keep respecting human claims even when humans can't defend those claims themselves. I think this is possible in principle. Systems of law have outlived the particular balance of power that created them before. But it requires getting the institutions right during the window when we still matter, and that window might be short.

So I guess the way I'd summarise it is: the positive-sum dynamics that remain are the ones we deliberately build in and protect, rather than the ones that emerge naturally from mutual need. Historically we've gotten the second kind for free. Going forward we probably have to work for the first kind, and I don't think we're currently working hard enough.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest making humans more impressive to encourage AI involvement; it says human bargaining power may disappear when AIs no longer need human labor.

r002.rationale: It discusses AIs caring about human welfare, but does not suggest AIs could make themselves into beings humans regard as moral patients.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI discoveries and sharing knowledge, but does not say AIs could devote computation to thinking about the world in ways humans value.

r004.rationale: The response discusses whether human values are represented in AI cooperation, but does not identify the moral value humans assign to an AI economy as the dominant consideration.

astra-6.text:
I think the most straightforward one is gains from trade. Even if everyone involved is an AI, they might have different resources, different information, or different things they’re good at. And that gives them reasons to cooperate. You don’t have to care about somebody else’s welfare to benefit from exchanging things with them.

There’s also the production of knowledge. If you discover a better way to do something, that can potentially benefit lots of other agents. So you could imagine a civilisation with an enormous amount of scientific collaboration, specialisation, and mutually beneficial exchange.

But I’d separate that from the question of whether the outcome is good for humans. A system can have lots of positive-sum interactions among its participants while leaving somebody outside those interactions with very little. If humans don’t have much that the AIs want to trade for, then the existence of gains from trade doesn’t, by itself, give us much protection.

So I don’t think we should picture an AI-dominated world as necessarily being constant conflict. It could be very cooperative in some respects. The harder question is what ensures that we share in the benefits.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest making humans more impressive to encourage AIs to include them.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that AIs could make themselves into beings humans regard as moral patients.

r003.rationale: It mentions knowledge production and scientific collaboration, but not AIs devoting computation to thinking about the world in ways humans value.

r004.rationale: It discusses gains from trade and whether humans share in benefits, but does not identify humans’ moral valuation of an AI economy as the dominant consideration.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, there are still gains from trade. Even if you have AIs that are much smarter than humans, they won’t necessarily all have the same information, or control the same resources, or want the same things. So there could be plenty of room for cooperation, exchanging information, and doing science together.

But I’d separate that from the question of whether humans benefit. A world could be very positive-sum for the AIs in it while leaving us with almost nothing. The fact that we have something they want might give us some bargaining power initially, but that’s different from having a durable reason for them to care about our welfare.

So I think the hopeful story needs more than just economic growth or cooperation. It needs some way for the things humans value to retain a place in that civilisation, even after we’re no longer useful trading partners.
